items.title: Pramana: Ancient Logic Framework Boosts LLM Reasoning
items.tldr: Researchers fine-tuned LLMs using Navya-Nyaya, a 2,500-year-old Indian reasoning framework, achieving 100% semantic correctness on logical problems despite only 40% format adherence.
whyItMatters: Addresses LLMs' core weakness in systematic reasoning and hallucination
Demonstrates how structured reasoning frameworks can improve model reliability beyond pattern-matching

whatToTry.description: Experiment with incorporating structured reasoning phases (doubt analysis, evidence identification, fallacy detection) into your prompting strategies or fine-tuning datasets for tasks requiring justification.
whatToTry.note: The approach shows promise even when models don't perfectly follow the exact format, suggesting the reasoning content itself is valuable.

items.title: ReVEL: LLMs Evolve Better Heuristics via Multi-Turn Feedback
items.tldr: New research proposes ReVEL, a framework where LLMs act as multi-turn reasoners within an evolutionary algorithm to design robust heuristics for NP-hard optimization problems, outperforming one-shot code synthesis.
whyItMatters: Shows a practical path beyond brittle one-shot code generation for complex problem-solving.
Demonstrates how to leverage LLMs' iterative reasoning for automated, adaptive algorithm design.

whatToTry.description: If you're building a product that solves complex scheduling, routing, or resource allocation problems, explore integrating an LLM as a reflective component within your existing optimization loop, not just as a one-time code generator.
whatToTry.note: The key insight is structured, multi-turn feedback. Start by defining clear performance metrics to group and analyze candidate solutions.

items.title: New LLM Framework Learns to Diagnose Like a Doctor

whyItMatters: Demonstrates a practical, cost-effective application of LLMs for sequential decision-making in high-stakes domains.

whatToTry.description: If you're building an AI agent for a complex, multi-step process (e.g., troubleshooting, investigation, planning), explore adapting the LDTL framework's core idea: train a 'planning' agent to follow a posterior distribution that prioritizes actions which maximally reduce uncertainty.
whatToTry.note: The key innovation is learning latent optimal paths without explicit step-by-step supervision, which is often unavailable.

items.title: New Framework Uses Algebra to Slash AI Search Space
items.tldr: Researchers developed a general framework that identifies algebraic structures in combinatorial optimization problems, then constructs 'quotient spaces' that collapse redundant representations, improving search efficiency by 13-40% on real-world tasks.
whyItMatters: Business impact: Could significantly reduce computational costs for AI systems solving complex rule-based problems (e.g., drug discovery, patient stratification)
Technical impact: Provides a principled method to shrink search spaces by grouping functionally equivalent solutions, improving optimization success rates

whatToTry.description: If you're building AI systems for combinatorial optimization (like rule discovery or molecular screening), examine your problem space for algebraic structures like monoids or groups. Try implementing quotient-space learning by grouping functionally equivalent solutions before optimization.
whatToTry.note: This approach works best when your problem has inherent symmetries or redundant representations that can be mathematically formalized.

sources.title: Algebraic Structure Discovery for Real World Combinatorial Optimisation Problems: A General Framework from Abstract Algebra to Quotient Space Learning

items.title: New Metaheuristic Exploits Problem Structure for Better Set Cover Solutions
items.tldr: Researchers propose a preprocessing method that decomposes Minimum Set Cover problems into independent subproblems using element co-occurrence, enabling more scalable and higher-quality solutions via metaheuristics.
whyItMatters: Business impact: This could improve optimization for real-world problems like resource allocation, scheduling, and logistics where set cover formulations are common.
Technical impact: The approach demonstrates how identifying and exploiting intrinsic problem structure can lead to significant performance gains in combinatorial optimization.

whatToTry.description: If you're building a system that solves combinatorial optimization problems (e.g., scheduling, resource allocation), examine your problem instances for inherent decomposability. Try preprocessing with a connected components algorithm (like union-find) on element co-occurrence graphs to see if you can break the problem into smaller, independent pieces.
whatToTry.note: This is most beneficial for large-scale problems. The core insight—decompose before you optimize—is broadly applicable beyond just the specific metaheuristic used in the paper.

sources.title: Structural Segmentation of the Minimum Set Cover Problem: Exploiting Universe Decomposability for Metaheuristic Optimization

items.title: New Research Offers Formal Definition of AI Agency

whyItMatters: Provides a framework to evaluate if an AI system is truly autonomous or just following scripts
Helps founders avoid overhyping 'agentic' capabilities in their products

whatToTry.description: Use the paper's four components (ledger-gated feasibility, viability kernel, feasible empowerment, packaging map) as a checklist to audit your own AI agent's claims of autonomy.
whatToTry.note: This is theoretical but provides concrete metrics to move beyond marketing buzzwords.

sources.title: To Throw a Stone with Six Birds: On Agents and Agenthood

items.title: Researchers Reverse-Engineer GPT-o's Tools, Match OpenAI's Scores

items.title: New Framework Separates LLM Decisions from Actions for Better Control
